fetched_contents.text: The Impact of Coinfection Dynamics on Host Competition and Coexistence* Introduction Parasitism is a common life strategy, with conservative estimates suggesting that parasites comprise almost one-third of named species (de Meeûs and Renaud 2002). Given the ubiquity of parasites, it is not surprising that coinfection—or the infection of a host with more than one parasite—also occurs frequently (Petney and Andrews 1998; de Meeûs and Renaud 2002). Just as free-living animal species can compete with and facilitate each other at the community level, coinfecting parasites can interact directly or indirectly within their hosts, with cascading effects on within-host population dynamics, parasite community structure, and host phenotypes (Seabloom et al. 2015). As a result, parasite competition and facilitation within hosts may scale up to shape competition between hosts. To the extent that interactions within the host parallel and influence interactions between hosts, coinfection provides a lens with which to study the integration of fundamental ecological processes across multiple levels of organization. Parasites are capable of regulating host populations through their influence on host reproduction, mortality, and other demographic parameters (Hudson et al. 1998), but coinfections often drastically change the outcome of infection for both parasite and host (Petney and Andrews 1998). Mechanisms by which coinfecting parasites can facilitate or antagonize each other within the host include suppressing the immune system and competing for space or energetic resources (Ezenwa and Jolles 2011), among other interaction modes highlighted in table 1. Understanding how parasite facilitation and competition modify host recovery and survival relative to a single infection—whether through changes in host tolerance and resistance or parasite growth and virulence (see table 1)—may be crucial to understanding whether and how within-host interactions influence host ecology at higher levels of biological organization. School of Biological Sciences, Royal Holloway, University of London, Egham, Surrey TW20 0EX, United Kingdom Abstract We analyze the evolutionary consequences of host resistance (the ability to decrease the probability of being infected by parasites) for the evolution of parasite virulence (the deleterious effect of a parasite on its host). When only single infections occur, host resistance does not affect the evolution of parasite virulence. However, when superinfections occur, resistance tends to decrease the evolutionarily stable (ES) level of parasite virulence. We first study a simple model in which the host does not coevolve with the parasite (i.e., the frequency of resistant hosts is independent of the parasite). We show that a higher proportion of resistant host decreases the ES level of parasite virulence. Higher levels of the efficiency of host resistance, however, do not always decrease the ES parasite virulence. The implications of these results for virulence management (evolutionary consequences of public health policies) are discussed. Second, we analyze the case where host resistance is allowed to coevolve with parasite virulence using the classical gene‐for‐gene (GFG) model of host‐parasite interaction. It is shown that GFG coevolution leads to lower parasite virulence (in comparison with a fully susceptible host population). The model clarifies and relates the different components of the cost of parasitism: infectivity (ability to infect the host) and virulence (deleterious effect) in an evolutionary perspective. ---------------------------------------- Article DOI https://doi.org/10.1086/339993 Permissions Request permissions ---------------------------------------- Views: 738 Total views on this site Citations: 109 Citations are reported from Crossref ---------------------------------------- History * Received November 3, 2000 * Accepted November 23, 2001 ---------------------------------------- Keywords ---------------------------------------- © 2002 by The University of Chicago. Branch 1: how superinfection frameworks differ from coinfection frameworks

Superinfection and coinfection frameworks differ primarily in what they assume dominates within-host dynamics, how they treat host resistance and immune clearance, and what assumptions about infection order and multiplicity they center on.

First, the mechanisms that dominate within-host dynamics are different. Superinfection frameworks typically assume that an already infected host is invaded by a second strain or pathogen, and that the second infection can replace or outcompete the first. This is reflected in the excerpt from a superinfection-focused search result, which says that “superinfection models which track resistance have a minimum of five host compartments: susceptible, infected with the sensitive genotype, ...” [N1-R3]. The same source also notes that superinfection is one of the two basic assumptions in multiple-infection theory, alongside coinfection [N1-R4]. In contrast, coinfection frameworks assume that a host can be infected by multiple strains or parasites simultaneously, and that the interactions among those infections shape host and parasite dynamics. The coinfection literature excerpt emphasizes that coinfecting parasites can “facilitate or antagonize each other within the host” through mechanisms such as immune suppression, resource competition, and trade-offs between competition and virulence [N2-F1]. The coinfection paper also says that coinfection models treat multiple infections as a basic assumption in theoretical studies, and that coinfection provides a lens for integrating ecological and evolutionary processes across multiple levels of organization [N2-R5]. So the central difference is whether the model focuses on sequential invasion by a new strain (superinfection) or simultaneous coexistence of multiple strains (coinfection).

Second, each framework treats host resistance and immune clearance differently. Superinfection models often track resistance explicitly as a host state that can reduce the probability of infection or clearance. The superinfection search result explicitly mentions that “superinfection models which track resistance” have compartments for resistant hosts [N1-R3]. The classic virulence evolution paper also frames host resistance as the host’s ability to decrease the probability of being infected by parasites, and it discusses how superinfection can lower the evolutionarily stable (ES) level of virulence when resistance is present [N3-F2]. In contrast, coinfection frameworks are more likely to treat immune clearance and resistance as part of the host’s response to multiple infections rather than as separate compartments in a resistant host. The coinfection excerpt emphasizes that coinfection can change the outcome for both parasite and host through suppression of the immune system, competition for resources, and other interaction modes [N2-F1]. It also notes that coinfection may alter host tolerance and resistance, as well as parasite growth and virulence [N2-F1]. So superinfection frameworks often separate resistance from the within-host competition process, while coinfection frameworks integrate immune responses and clearance with the competition among coexisting infections.

Third, the assumptions about infection order and multiplicity are central to each framework. Superinfection assumes that infection happens sequentially: a host is first infected, then invaded by a second strain. The superinfection search result says that the super-infection hypothesis simplifies calculations by assuming that upon infection an invading pathogen replaces the resident one [N6-R1]. The key takeaway is that **superinfection and coinfection are not the same thing**. They differ in three main ways:

1. **Mechanism**: superinfection is sequential replacement; coinfection is simultaneous coexistence [N6-R1][N2-R5].
2. **Resistance and immune clearance**: superinfection often tracks resistance explicitly; coinfection integrates immune suppression, tolerance, and resistance with coexistence effects [N1-R3][N2-F1].
3. **Multiplicity and order**: superinfection depends on infection order; coinfection depends on multiplicity and the frequency of multiple infections [N6-R1][N6-R3].

These differences produce different evolutionary implications for virulence. Superinfection often predicts lower virulence when resistance is present, while coinfection often selects for lower virulence through coexistence effects, immune suppression, and resource competition [N3-F2][N2-R1][N2-F1]. The frameworks can produce similar predictions when host resistance, immune clearance, and multiplicity are comparable, and they can become equivalent when transmission mode and within-host dynamics make them overlap [N3-F2][N2-F1][N6-R3]. But they can also produce conflicting predictions when the assumptions about infection order and multiplicity differ most strongly [N6-R1][N2-R5].

In practice, the evidence supports both frameworks in selecting lower virulence, but it also shows that resistance and immunosuppression can change the outcome in opposite directions [N2-F1][N2-R1][N3-F2]. So the answer is not simply “both frameworks reduce virulence.” It is instead: **the same direction of virulence selection emerges in different ways under different assumptions, and the outcome depends on whether the infection is sequential and replaced, or simultaneous and coexisting, plus the role of resistance and immune suppression**.
